text: Today, you will watch a person, Sarah, participate in an easter egg hunt. This is what a field looks like:

To prepare for the easter egg hunt, this morning the farmer had to put together all of the plastic eggs, and place them in his fields.

He hid one prize in each field. The prize is always a silver token. So no matter how many easter eggs are in a field, only one egg has the silver token prize inside.

To show you which egg has the prize, we'll circle it like this:

This morning, Sarah was wandering around the farm as the farmer was hiding the eggs. Sometimes, she SAW the farmer set up some of the eggs in a field.

If Sarah saw the farmer set up an egg, she knows if it's empty, or if it has a prize hidden inside.

Because the grass isn't very tall, Sarah can see where all of the eggs are inside a field.

BUT, Sarah may not know where the prize is. Even though the prize egg is circled here, it's obviously not circled for Sarah. So Sarah only knows where the prize is if she saw the farmer hide it.

Sarah only saw the farmer set up some of the eggs. Sometimes, Sarah knows a lot about a field:

For example, here Sarah knows that some of the eggs do not have the prize, but doesn't know where the prize is between the remaining eggs.

And sometimes Sarah doesn't know much about a field:

For any given egg, there is a 50/50 chance Sarah saw inside (and knows if it has the prize).

When it's time for the easter egg hunt, the farmer always gives Sarah a choice. There are always two fields, and Sarah needs to choose which one to search for the prize.

She can either choose to search the field on the left, or the field on the right. Sarah can only search the field she chooses.

The arrow shows which field Sarah chose. Here, Sarah chose the field on the left

Sarah wants to find the prize as quickly and easily as possible. So she wants to choose the field where it will be easiest for her to get the prize.

The fewer eggs are hidden in a field, the quicker Sarah will be able to search them. And the closer to the entrance they are, the quicker Sarah will be able to reach them.

So both the number of eggs, and their distance from the entrance, affect how hard it is to search a field.

Also, the more Sarah knows about the location of the prize, the easier it may be for her to find it.

Importantly, Sarah does not necessarily know the same amount about each field; she may know more or less about one field than the other.

So to recap: Sarah always wants to choose the field where she will find the prize the quickest, and with the least effort.

To decide which field to search, she needs to consider:

1. How much she knows about each field.

2. How many eggs are in each field. The more eggs Sarah doesn't know about, the harder she may have to work to find the egg with the prize.

3. How far the eggs are from the entrance of each field. The farther Sarah has to walk to search for or retrieve the prize, the harder she has to work.

And Sarah has a 50/50 chance of knowing what's inside any given egg.

Your task: You are going to see what Sarah chooses to do in different situations. So you will see if Sarah decides to search field A, or field B.

Your goal is to figure out how much Sarah knew about the location of the prize in each field. For each field, you will rate: From 0 (Sarah has no idea which egg has the prize inside) to 100 (Sarah knows exactly where the prize is): how much information did Sarah already know about the prize's location?

Great job!

So there are three really important things to remember:

1. Sarah might know a lot about the prize's location in a field, she might not know much, or she might know something in between.

2. Sarah does not necessarily know the same amount about each field.

3. In each case, Sarah needs to decide which field to search for the prize.

To show YOU which egg has the prize, we'll circle it. But remember, Sarah can't see these circles.

For any given egg, there is only a 50/50 chance Sarah saw inside (and knows if it has the prize).

You are going to see which field Sarah chooses to search in different situations. So you will see if Sarah decides to search the field to the left, or the field to the right

For each field, you will rate: From 0 (Sarah has no idea which egg has the prize inside) to 100 (Sarah knows exactly where the prize is): how much information did Sarah already know about the prize's location?

You will always be asked to rate how much Sarah knows about the field to the left first, and then the field to the right second. Please pay attention and make sure to match each question to the correct field.
